_comment: Player contract: bump whenever pack.ts starts emitting something an older player/game.js cannot read. The player build stamps this into public/player/build.json; publishClient refuses to publish when the two disagree, and the player refuses to boot a game.bin from a newer packer. v1 = every bundle built before the guard existed (no build.json at all) -- notably the 2026-07-22 bundle that predates terrain heightChunk/splatChunk and animation-field playback. v3 adds tilemap cell chunks: a v2 player ignores `chunk` on a tile chunk and would render an empty map with nothing logged, which is exactly the silent failure this number exists to prevent. v4 moves UI out of `scenes[].ui` and into UI nodes in the scene tree: a v3 player has no UI node classes, so parseNodeJson falls through to Node.parse and the game renders no HUD at all, silently -- again exactly what this number exists to catch. v5 moves SHARED animation clips out of the serialized nodes and into a game-level `animations` array (with `modelAnimations` saying which model plays which), retargeted onto each character at load: a v4 player never runs that step, so every character that uses a shared clip stands in its bind pose with nothing logged. v6 moves a skinned model's per-vertex bone data (`jointIndices`/`jointWeights`) out of the manifest JSON and into blob chunks, because Model.serialize now writes those as typed arrays and a typed array stringifies as {"0":..} rather than an array: a v5 player finds neither the chunk it does not know about nor a readable array, so every skinned character loads with no bone weights and collapses to the origin -- silently, which is what this number exists to catch. v7 adds NavMeshNode: a v6 player has no such class, so parseNodeJson falls through to Node.parse, scene.navMeshes comes back empty, and every controller on a `path` or `patrol` goal falls back to walking in a straight line into the geometry it was supposed to route around -- silently, which is what this number exists to catch. v8 adds DecalNode: a v7 player has no such class, so parseNodeJson falls through to Node.parse, each decal loads as a plain Node with its `decal` payload dropped, and every scorch mark, painted road line and area-of-effect ring is missing from the published game -- silently, which is what this number exists to catch. v9 replaces the terrain's 4-layer normalized splat with a layer STACK: a base landscape material plus ordered paint layers, each with a mask channel in a `masksChunk`, and slot rules evaluated in the shader. A v8 player knows `splatChunk` and four `layers`, finds neither, and draws every landscape in its base colour with no painted roads, no rules and no foliage rules bound to a layer -- silently, which is what this number exists to catch. v10 adds controller LAYERS, action SLOTS, pose states, clip-owned events and skeleton SOCKETS (`stateMachine.layers/slots`, `state.pose`, `animation.events`, `skin.sockets`, node `socketAttachment`): a v9 player ignores all of them, so an upper-body layer never plays, a held weapon stays where it was placed instead of following the hand, and footstep events on clips never fire -- silently, which is what this number exists to catch. v11 adds ParticleSystemNode and ForceFieldNode: a v10 player has no such classes, so parseNodeJson falls through to Node.parse, each loads as a plain Node with its `particleSystem` / `forceField` payload dropped, and every fire, spark, smoke plume and wind zone is missing from the published game -- silently, which is what this number exists to catch. v12 adds WaterVolumeNode: a v11 player has no such class, so parseNodeJson falls through to Node.parse, the `waterVolume` payload is dropped, and nothing floats -- crates and logs sink through the pond and the surface never ripples -- silently, which is what this number exists to catch. v13 adds anatomical ragdoll profiles (skin.ragdollProfile, ragdollProfile.ts): a v12 player has no profile builder, so every death falls as the old generic per-bone ragdoll -- 1 kg spheres on the joints, knees bending both ways -- with nothing to say why. v14 gives every scene its own render settings (`scenes[].render`), applied as the player starts it: a v13 player ignores them, so a game that walks from a daylit valley into a dark dungeon shows the dungeon through the valley's exposure, shadows and post -- black, or blown out -- silently, which is what this number exists to catch. v15 adds ExposureVolumeNode: a v14 player has no such class, so parseNodeJson falls through to Node.parse, the `exposureVolume` payload is dropped, and a cave or interior authored with its own exposure is shown through the scene-wide exposure instead -- blown out or crushed -- silently, which is what this number exists to catch. v16 adds ClothNode: a v15 player has no such class, so parseNodeJson falls through to Node.parse, the `cloth` payload is dropped, and every cape, banner and flag is missing from the published game -- silently, which is what this number exists to catch. v17 adds trigger OPTIONS (`trigger.enabled/group/mask/detectTriggers/continuous`) and trigger-to-trigger overlaps: a v16 player ignores them, so every trigger loads enabled, in layer 1, detecting only moving bodies -- a hurtbox never sees a hitbox and a switched-off hitbox is live -- and a combat game deals no damage at all, silently, which is what this number exists to catch. v18 replaces OccluderNode with OcclusionVolumeNode (type `occlusionVolume`): a box whose CONTENTS are skipped while the box cannot be seen, where an `occluder` hid what was BEHIND it. A v17 player has no such class, so parseNodeJson falls through to Node.parse and the volume hides nothing -- silently slower, never wrong -- while a v17 player reading a legacy `occluder` would rasterize a volume fitted round a room as a solid wall and cull what you can see past it, which is what this number exists to catch. v19 adds VolumetricFogNode (type `volumetricFog`), moonlight in lux (`atmosphere.moonIlluminance`), physical sky units (`atmosphere.physicalUnits`), light flicker (`light.flicker`) and light-following sprites and particle systems (`followLight`, `fogGlow`): a v18 player has no fog class, so parseNodeJson falls through to Node.parse and every fog bank is missing, and it reads a lux moon as the default fraction of the sun -- a moon as bright as day -- silently, which is what this number exists to catch. v20 makes WeatherNode a bounded box volume (`weather.size/blendDistance/priority/enabled`), several of which may overlap, adds puddles, a snow material (`weather.snowMaterial`, `snowMaterialId`, `snowTiling/Slope/Breakup`) and shelter (`weather.shelter`), and draws wetness and snow on the landscape: a v19 player reads a bounded volume as scene-wide weather on the foliage alone, so a snowy hilltop box snows every plant in the game and leaves the ground bare -- silently, which is what this number exists to catch. v21 adds the AgX Punchy tone mapper (`render.toneMapper: 'agxPunchy'`) and makes the physical sky's march converge, calibrated to measured daylight: a v20 player has no such curve and falls back to plain AgX, so the clear sky turns steel-grey again, and it marches a physical sky in even steps to its atmosphere's top, so a thick atmosphere comes out up to 17 times too dark -- silently, which is what this number exists to catch. v22 turns cylindrical sprites to face the camera's POSITION about their own upright axis (they lay parallel to the screen, squashed and leaning at the corners of a wide view), shadows light-probe captures with a sun map of their own, keeps a deferred probe slot for the unbounded fallback probe and hands the other to the volume the camera is in, takes a normal map's lost mip detail into the roughness, fixes the split-sum Fresnel that made rough ground glossy at grazing angles, and floors a lit smoke sprite's local lights at its own thickness: a v21 player draws the same game with sprites lying flat to the screen, probes lit through their own hills and roofs, and a white orb in the smoke over every fire at night -- silently, which is what this number exists to catch. v23 applies a light probe's LIGHTING per pixel from every lighting probe in view, as spherical harmonics in the deferred pass's uniform block (and per draw for forward materials, per effect for lit particles and sprites), where it used to come from the two cubemap slots handed out by the camera's position; the slots now carry reflections alone: a v22 player lights a room from its probe only while the camera stands inside it, so a house looked into through its door is lit like the street and darkens with a jump on the threshold -- silently, which is what this number exists to catch. v24 applies probe REFLECTIONS per pixel from one octahedral reflection atlas (and box-projects them, `lightProbe.boxProjection`), bakes and relights probes in time-sliced jobs, and leaves lights with `light.bake` false out of probe captures: a v23 player reflects whatever probe box the camera stands in on every surface, ignores box projection and the bake flag, and captures every probe whole in one frame -- a hitch each time the sun moves -- silently, which is what this number exists to catch. v25 adds GIVolumeNode (type `giVolume`) and the GI bakes game.bin carries (`giBakes`): a v24 player has no such class, so parseNodeJson falls through to Node.parse, the `giVolume` payload is dropped, and every room a GI volume lights is lit by the open sky's fill through its roof instead -- silently, which is what this number exists to catch. v26 adds a WeatherNode's falling rain and snow (`weather.precipitation`, `precipitationRate/Size/Speed/Wind/Sprite`), run by the scene as particle systems round the camera that stop under shelter, and the raindrops that ripple puddles and hit the wet landscape while it rains: a v25 player reads none of it, so a rainy scene is wet but nothing falls and its puddles lie still -- silently, which is what this number exists to catch. v27 adds AREA lights (`lightType: 'area'`, `light.shape/width/height/twoSided`) and GI volume probe insets (`giVolume.probeInset`), and GI bakes of format 2: a v26 player throws on the unknown light type and stops loading the scene, and stands every inset volume's probes on its faces, where they see through floors and walls -- which is what this number exists to catch. v28 adds SEQUENCE nodes (`type: 'sequence'`, an embedded `sequence` plus slot `bindings`), the cinematic sequencer: a v27 player parses them as plain nodes, so a game that opens on a cinematic, or plays one from a menu, shows nothing and its camera never moves -- silently, which is what this number exists to catch. v29 makes 2D scenes (`scene.dimension: '2D'`, stamped on every 2D scene root) draw through the flat 2D frame -- one sorted pass of tiles, sprites and particles, no 3D passes, a fixed exposure of 1 -- unless `render.pipeline2D` is 'full', and adds side-view sprite sorting on tilemaps (`tilemap.entitySort: 'none'`): a v28 player draws a 2D game through the 3D frame at the 3D exposure and Y-sorts a side-scroller's characters behind whatever stands below them -- silently, which is what this number exists to catch. v30 adds Camera2DNode (`camera2D`), Room2DNode (`room2D`) and ParallaxLayerNode (`parallaxLayer`), tileset `pixelsPerUnit` and `regions`, and sprite `pivot`/`flipX`/`flipY`: a v29 player has no such classes, so the 2D camera loads as a plain node and the game shows the world from nowhere, rooms and backdrops vanish, and every pixel-sized sprite draws as a unit square at its centre -- silently, which is what this number exists to catch. v31 adds the 2D physics: CharacterBody2DNode (`characterBody2D`), Body2DNode (`body2D`) and Area2DNode (`area2D`), tile `oneWay`/`slope`, and tilemap `colliders3D`: a v30 player has no such classes, so every 2D character loads as a plain node that never moves, falls or collides, and a map with its 3D colliders off has no collision at all -- silently, which is what this number exists to catch. v32 adds sprite animation sets on AnimatedSpriteNode (`animationSet`, `animationSetId`): named clips with frame times, events and hitboxes, and a sprite state machine: a v31 player plays only the node's single frame list, so a 2D character stands on one frame list whatever it does, its attack hitboxes never switch on and its frame events never fire -- silently, which is what this number exists to catch. v33 adds a 2D body's `oneWayPlatforms` switch (`characterBody2D.oneWayPlatforms: false`): a v32 player stands every flier on the one-way platforms it should pass through, so a bat hovers on a plank above the player it is chasing and never reaches them -- silently, which is what this number exists to catch. v34 moves the 2D platformer out of the engine: a Character Body 2D (`characterBody2D`) now carries generic walk/fly locomotion (`movement`, `walkSpeed`, `runSpeed`, `jumpHeight`, `jumpTimeToApex`, `coyoteSeconds`, `jumpBufferSeconds`, ...) and is driven by a possessing Controller node, its dash, double jump and wall jump written in the game's script (`onMove2D`): a v33 player has neither the 2D possession nor the new fields, so the player character stands still and every enemy floats -- silently, which is what this number exists to catch. v35 lets an AI Controller drive a 2D body: it sees across the picture plane, through the 2D world, the bodies on its `perceptionLayers` (`controller.perceptionLayers`), steers a walker along X and a flier in XY, and reads the new senses `wallAhead`, `ledgeAhead` and `targetInFront`: a v34 player has no 2D perception or steering, so every 2D enemy stands still, and a guard that is given a layer mask sees its own kind -- silently, which is what this number exists to catch. v36 adds 2D navigation: a NavMeshNode in 2D space (`navMesh.space: '2D'`, `agent2D`, a baked `graph2D` of walks, jumps, drops and drop-throughs, or an air grid) that 2D controllers path, patrol and investigate on, jumping where a leg says: a v35 player has no 2D graph, so every 2D `path` falls back to walking straight at its target and no enemy ever jumps to a platform -- silently, which is what this number exists to catch. v37 makes colliders and triggers NODES: a Collider (`type: 'collider'`, a `collider` block of the old body's settings plus `layer`/`mask` and its `shapes`) IS the rigid body and carries what is under it, a Trigger (`type: 'trigger'`, a `sensor` block) is the sensor -- a 3D one in a 3D scene, the 2D area in a 2D one -- and a Character takes its body from the Collider it stands in; a node's `body`/`trigger` properties and Area 2D nodes convert on load: a v36 player has no Collider or Trigger class, so parseNodeJson falls through to Node.parse and nothing is solid, nothing falls, no trigger fires and no character moves -- silently, which is what this number exists to catch. v38 splits the player into ES modules: game.js is a module entry that loads the engine in chunks/, the physics worker is physics-worker.js beside it (no longer inlined), and build.json lists the core files and each optional part's (the Rapier and Jolt backends), which a publish copies: a v37 publish path would copy game.js alone, and the game would stop on its first import with nothing on screen but the loading spinner -- which is what this number exists to catch. v39 moves the shaders out of the player and into game.bin: the published player imports each shader as a handle onto the library a game carries (manifest.shaders, src/graphics/shaderLibrary.ts), and a publish ships each program's base and only the variants its program list names. A v38 packer writes no shaders, and a v39 player could build no program from its game -- it says so instead of drawing nothing. v40 splits the engine's optional features (Project ▸ Features) out of the player's core into chunks of their own, which the player loads from config.features before it builds the engine: a v39 player has every feature in its core and ignores config.features, but a v40 game published with a feature left out ships without that feature's chunk, which only a v40 player knows to go without. v41 adds clip foot-lock windows (`animation.footLocks`): per foot, the spans in which foot placement may lock it. A v40 player ignores them and decides by itself when each foot is planted, holding feet to toe-off the windows were drawn to release at heel-off -- silently, which is what this number exists to catch. v42 adds animator state GROUPS (`stateMachine.groups`, `layer.groups`: a transition from a group fires from any of its states, one into a group enters its entry), and states that hold the character still (`state.holdMovement`): a v41 player finds no state of a group's name, so a character in a turn, a stop or a landing never takes its group's way out and stands in it for good, and a hard landing slides on with the stick -- silently, which is what this number exists to catch. v43 plays blend spaces on ADDITIVE layers (a look-at: pose clips blended by the aim, added over each sample's own first frame) and waits `turnSettleFarSeconds` before a 180 turn in place: a v42 player adds nothing from an additive blend-space layer, so a character that should look round with its head stares ahead, and turns its body at once when the camera swings behind -- silently, which is what this number exists to catch. v43 also passes a player Controller's camera pitch on as the aim's (`aimPitch`), which a v42 player left at 0, so the same character never looks up or down; and a state held at speed 0 blends in, which in a v42 player it never finished doing; and its foot IK turns a knee's pole smoothly, never pulls a leg straight with a lock that is letting go, and reads `lockCatchSpeed`, without which a strafing knee flips and the legs snap. v44 moves the script decorators (@attribute, @onAction, @child, @save, ...) out of the 'cleo' module and into 'cleo/decorators', which scripts now import them from: a v43 player has no 'cleo/decorators' module, so every script that uses a decorator stops on its first import and its node does nothing at all -- which is what this number exists to catch. v45 has camera rigs pick collision layers: a rig's `collisionLayers` (Blocked by) and `seeThroughLayers` (See through) replace its `collisionMode`, a Collider's layer replaces its `cameraCollision` and the per-node and per-foliage-rule `cameraDither`, and foot IK rigs trace only their `traceLayers`: a v44 player reads every rig as 'retract', so the boom catches on the small props, stair ramps and see-through pillars it should pass, and feet land on the ramp laid over a flight of stairs instead of its steps -- silently, which is what this number exists to catch. v46 adds animator SYNC GROUPS (`state.syncGroup`: a transition between two states of one group starts the state entered at the phase the one left was at, and the two blend spaces run on one phase through the cross-fade) and the Character's slope hold (`character.slopeLimit`, 45 degrees unless set: gravity only presses a character standing on ground up to that steep into it), and a state that plants by its clips' foot-lock windows (`state.plantInWindows`) leaves a foot inside one planted at any height: a v45 player starts every blend space at phase 0, so a walk handing over to a stair climb swaps its legs mid-stride, a character standing on a ramp creeps down it, and a stair climb's upper foot floats over its tread -- silently, which is what this number exists to catch. v47 adds vehicles a Controller possesses (its intent drives one: move steers and throttles, `jumpHeld` holds the hand brake), `vehicle.parked` and the drivetrain written as `drivetrain`, a Collider body switched off at runtime (`physicsEnabled`, kept out of the world while its node is carried), and root motion that composes travel with the turn already applied: a v46 player leaves a parked car rolling, ignores a Controller that possesses a vehicle, and walks a clip that turns and travels off its path -- silently, which is what this number exists to catch. v48 has a LAYER state in the base layer's sync group follow the base's phase every frame (`state.syncGroup` on a layer: an upper-body layer keeps step with the legs whatever its clips' lengths): a v47 player runs such a layer on its own clock, so a weapon held over the stride drifts out of step with the legs and the torso twists against the hips -- silently, which is what this number exists to catch. v48 also adds POSE samples in blend spaces (`sample.pose`, the field's pose table `field.poses` whose variants name their `base`), poses measured from their base on additive layers (`pose.reference`), STEADY layer states (`state.meshSpace`: the pose keeps its own model-space turn at the top of its mask) and support-hand IK on a layer (`layer.handIk`): a v47 player plays a pose sample as a missing clip, so a weapon hold and its aim offset show nothing, and the rifle's chest swings with the hips and the left hand comes off it -- silently, which is what this number exists to catch. v49 adds the native attribute types: a script field typed with an engine asset class (`skin: Material`, `icon: Texture`, `hit: Sound`, `tiles: Tileset`) is stored as `{ $asset, id }` and a node-class field (`lamp: LightNode`) as `{ $nodePath }`, which the engine turns into the asset and the node as the script attaches and starts, materials and tilesets coming from the game's one asset table (`assets`): a v48 player never resolves them, so every such field holds a plain object, and the first script that calls a method on its material, plays its sound or reads its node stops with a TypeError -- which is what this number exists to catch. v50 adds animator FORKS (`stateMachine.forks`, `layer.forks`): junctions a transition goes through, on to the first of the fork's ways out that holds, in the same frame, and a group whose `entry` is a fork: a v49 player finds no state of a fork's name, enters it as an empty state (the character drops to its bind pose for a frame, or a layer fades out) and takes the fork's ways out a frame late as that ghost state's own, so every jump, turn and stop of the Sandbox starts a frame late from the bind pose -- silently, which is what this number exists to catch. v51 adds STOP MOTION on animator states (`AnimationState.fps`, in `stateMachine.states` and every layer's states): the state's clips are sampled at a frame held for 1/fps of a second while its clock, events, root travel and cross-fades run on: a v50 player ignores the field and plays every such state smooth, so a game animated on twos ships fluid -- silently, which is what this number exists to catch. v52 wraps a custom material's CUBEMAP uniform (`samplerCube`, its texture id in `textures`) from the 2:1 panorama that id names onto a cube at runtime (render/panoramaCubes.ts, the `panoramaCube` program): a v51 player binds the panorama itself, a 2D texture, in the cube slot, which WebGPU rejects (the material draws nothing) and WebGL2 samples black -- silently, which is what this number exists to catch.
